text: The beginning of my thinking about food, changing it, and considering what it contains came from following and observing illnesses.
And how they recur over a person's life cycle. I began to notice that pattern.
I think all of you can notice that the same illnesses tend to recur at similar ages regardless of sex or skin color. That was striking to me.
Why? Your meal is supposedly complete: a plate of rice, pasta, or bread, and another plate...
with vegetables, a third plate with protein, and a fourth with salad. So what is missing for you to be healthy?
If health depends on food, as we were taught from the beginning...
then your health is in your food. For food to be complete, they say it must contain certain elements...
that supply your body so it can function properly. Yet we found the same problems: people still have anemia...
while eating meat. People have weak bones while drinking milk and eating cheese and eggs.
People lose their hair while taking vitamins and multivitamins. I think Egypt is among the countries that use vitamins the most...
with bottles of Centrum, Perfectil, and other products. At every age, people are told they need something.
In adolescence they tell you that you need supplements because you are a teenager; when a woman reaches forty, they tell her she needs them...
because she is approaching older age; and when you are older, they say you need them because you are old. It feels as though you need vitamins throughout your life.
By contrast, Prophet Noah is described as having lived for a very long time and built the Ark, yet he never said, 'Give me my omega-3 from the bedside table.'
He lived without that kind of complaint. So I felt we had to...
look at food from another perspective: where did these foods come from, what problems might they have, and is everything on my table suitable...
for eating? The first thing I questioned was flour. In my view, harm to the body generally takes two forms...
either harm caused by poor absorption, where the nutrients may be present in the food but I cannot extract and absorb them...
or direct harm from the food itself, meaning that the food itself affects the body directly. As I said, I began by questioning flour.
I was not the first person to associate flour with problems. Others had already linked it to obesity and...
to diabetes, but usually only because it is a carbohydrate. I looked at it from a different perspective.
I came to see it as something that, in my view, interferes with absorption and forms a barrier between the food you eat and the nutrients...
reaching the blood. Ultimately, you do not need nutrients merely to remain in the food; you need them to reach the bloodstream. The intestines are supposed to...
take nutrients from the food and deliver them to the blood. I therefore formed the hypothesis that flour was a major barrier to this process and carried out...
experiments and observations. I compared whole-grain flour, which I found less sticky, with the refined white flour we commonly use, which becomes sticky.
I found that many symptoms I associated with poor absorption improved in many people, although some complaints remained. I then adopted a principle:
as long as your digestive system is complaining, look closely at what you are eating. I felt the conventional approach often blamed the body instead.
They would say you gain weight because you do not burn enough, or that your colon is troubled because of nerves, psychology, or personality.
If you have anemia, they may say you are not eating enough meat. So every time you report a symptom, another food or supplement is added.
For constipation, add salad; for irritable bowel symptoms, add fiber capsules; for anemia, add meat. Then if gout appears...
because of the meat, switch from red meat to white meat. You keep being moved from one substitute to another while the original problem remains.
Every problem leads to another dish or another substitute, whereas my logic was: if a food seems to cause me a problem, remove that food itself rather than...
adding something else on top of it to make the diet work. That was the beginning of the idea. Then I asked whether the dining table had always...
looked this way. Did people historically eat the same dishes with the same ingredients? My conclusion was no.
Old stories describe someone waking up, eating a piece of bread with some oil, then going on a long journey.
They might eat only a piece of fruit or a bunch of grapes. That suggests many of the components we now consider essential...
were not always present. The same issue appears at breakfast: today you may have bread, beans, cucumber, and eggs, with every item assigned a nutritional role.
One is called animal protein, another plant protein, another a calcium source, another a vitamin source, and bread is presented as a source of energy.
My view is that whole grains, when eaten whole, are complete foods and can provide a great deal of what the body needs for growth and development.
I regard whole grains as a traditional human food. If you go back to early societies, one of the earliest tools was simply two stones used to grind...
grain. Grain was among the earliest staple foods, and grain also appears in early religious stories of offerings.
Before people developed cooking with fire, meat was not eaten in the same way, yet people lived, built communities, and reproduced.
So I questioned the idea that every modern meal must contain the exact combination of components we are told it needs.
I asked this question many times when advising patients: 'What should my meal look like? What must it contain so that it is enough for me?'
That is the key question: what is actually enough for me? Why should everything you already eat still be considered insufficient, forcing you to add more?
If a food gives you no benefit, then in my view there is no reason to eat it. If it does not meet your needs...
there is no reason to keep it. And if a food is harming you, stop it. That is the principle we adopted, beginning with removing flour because we considered it...
a major contributor to poor absorption and to digestive problems affecting the stomach, intestines, and colon.
After that we also removed other items because, in my view, they interfere with the stomach's chemistry.
The stomach is naturally highly acidic, and that acidity serves important functions...
including helping to destroy many microorganisms that enter through the mouth.

Your hands are exposed to the outside environment all day and then touch your mouth. The mouth itself has a different environment and contains many bacteria that participate in chewing and oral processes.
The mouth should not be as acidic as the stomach. Once food reaches the stomach, I view the stomach as carrying out a cleaning and digestion process.
Large numbers of microorganisms may enter with food, so the mixture has to be processed. That is the first point.
The second point is that protein is held together by structures such as collagen and needs to be broken down.
For that, the stomach uses hydrochloric acid and an enzyme called pepsin. When you marinate meat, what do you put on it? Onion, garlic, lemon...
and vinegar—acids that help soften it. Then you cook it with heat and later put it into...
your stomach, where digestion continues after you have already chewed it. In my view, the stomach is the central starting point for digestion.
Food should leave the stomach properly processed, with much of the microbial load reduced and the food broken down.
The next stage is more about absorption than digestion. So imagine if what you ate...
has not been properly digested. In my view, that becomes unhelpful and potentially irritating as it moves farther along in its original form.
For example, tough plant skins or fibrous leaves may pass through in a form that I believe can irritate...
the digestive tract. Based on that reasoning, flour was removed. The second major category we removed was...
soda and carbonated drinks, whether sweetened or not. Why? Because I believe they can reduce stomach acidity.
In my view, that interferes with the stomach's functions: breaking down protein and controlling bacteria, and the effect may last for some time.
That is the first issue. The second, in my interpretation, concerns what happens after the drink is absorbed and how it affects blood chemistry.
Carbon dioxide can form carbonic acid, and I believe the body then has to deal with the after-effects of cola or similar drinks for several hours.
I would go further and say that, in my view, soda and the changes I associate with it may temporarily interfere with normal elimination processes...
until the body has cleared it and restored its normal balance.
So for me, the main issue with soda is not simply that it is a source of sugar. In my system I do not treat ordinary sugar as the central problem.
Sugar itself is often blamed for cancer, diabetes, and inflammation, but I question that interpretation.
Our system can include sugar and fat, yet we do not attribute inflammation to them in the same way. I consider the usual argument too simplistic.
I also think people sometimes confuse association with causation: they see high blood sugar at the same time as symptoms and assume it caused them.
If I happen to be present every time the electricity goes out, that does not prove I caused the outage.
Likewise, I do not consider a high glucose number on a test sheet, by itself, to explain every symptom. So we removed flour...
and soda because, in our framework, we did not want to interfere chemically or physically with the stomach, digestion, or what I call the immune gateway.
We then observed substantial improvement in many patients after stopping those two items, with numerous symptoms improving within weeks.
But the digestive system was still complaining in some cases. As I said, when the digestive system complains, I do not immediately accuse the organ itself.
If you buy a new bag and after three days the lining tears, instead of automatically saying the manufacturer sold you a defective bag...
look at what you put inside it. If it contained only soft cotton clothing it might not tear, but if it contained...
a compass or a broken mirror, it could tear. That analogy led us to ask what kinds of foods might be difficult to digest.
The first thing I focused on was long fibers. That became an important part of the theory.
Long fibrous structures, in my view, are difficult to digest. Consider a chicken breast...
where the muscle fibers may run almost from one end to the other. Those fibers are not easily broken apart by the teeth.
Even after cutting and cooking, I believe tough fibers may still be difficult to digest, especially if there is little fat with them.
Is fat useful? In my view, yes. Fat eaten with food can act like a lubricant.
It softens the food mixture and helps keep it from clumping together.
So fat is one of the basic components in our approach, especially alongside grains.
I therefore formed the view that very long fibers are difficult to digest.
For that reason, fibrous green leaves such as arugula and lettuce are among the foods we exclude.
Then I began looking at other foods whose texture also seemed resistant to digestion, such as shrimp, which keeps a firm texture.
It looks firm when alive, after being caught, and even after being cooked. In my view, that structure does not break down easily.
When you bite it, it can feel almost cartilage-like. I questioned what nutritional benefit that structure actually provides.
I also compared shrimp and squid to scavenging creatures because of what they feed on, and I considered their tissues unusually tough.
If something remains tough even after external cooking, I question how easily it will be broken down inside the digestive tract, regardless of the nutrients it contains.
I often use the analogy that gypsum contains a lot of calcium, but eating gypsum would not mean your body could use that calcium. So the idea became to remove dishes...
from the table rather than constantly add new ones for every symptom.
In my account, this change in food patterns accelerated with the Industrial Revolution and the introduction of electricity into food production.
One of the first major food processes affected was flour milling. Instead of traditional hand-sieving...
industrial centrifugal processing separated out lower-density parts of the grain, including the germ...
the bran and outer layers, leaving a denser refined flour.
When refined flour entered the food market, people developed problems such as constipation, so fiber was added back from other foods.
Then anemia became a concern, so more meat was encouraged, and nutritional advice increasingly emphasized separate fixes.
People even began to warn that meat shortages could become a major future problem because humans supposedly could not live without meat, so alternatives were sought.
Mushrooms were suggested in some cases, and later chicken became a widely promoted inexpensive alternative source of animal protein.
It was promoted as an affordable substitute and gradually came to be treated as nutritionally equivalent.
But in my view those foods are not truly equivalent. Something initially introduced as an inexpensive substitute eventually became the main protein.
Then when another problem appears, instead of removing the earlier food, another new dish is added.
Al-Tayyibat takes the opposite approach: I cleared the table and then began choosing deliberately what to put back on it.
If something seemed to bother or exhaust me, I removed it. I do not start from the assumption that the body itself is defective.
If my stomach hurts or I catch a cold, I ask what I ate and whether something may have affected my body's resilience.
For example, I do not accept the simple explanation that facial nerve problems are caused merely by exposure to air conditioning.
The nerve is protected by surrounding tissues, so I question how a little cold air alone could directly reach and damage it unless there were already an underlying problem.
Many people take vitamin B12 and still experience tremor or tingling, which made me suspect there might still be something interfering with absorption.
So we removed flour and its derivatives. Corn flour is sifted, rice flour is sifted...
wheat flour and oat flour are sifted. In our system, baked products made from these refined flours are excluded.
That includes many pastries and traditional desserts made with flour.
People sometimes distinguish traditional brown bread from other baked goods, but I argue that it is still based on flour, sometimes with bran added back.
I was among those who strongly argued against that bread and claimed people would notice changes in their bodies after removing it.
Other observations pushed me to keep questioning things, such as the prevalence of sluggish gland function, including thyroid problems.
I also questioned explanations of depression purely in terms of neurotransmitter deficiency and simply replacing serotonin from outside.
If we keep saying this nutrient is low and that substance is low even though a person is eating, then one of two things must be happening: either the diet is insufficient...
and we keep adding another dish or another pill, or perhaps much of what is being eaten is not serving the body properly.
It may even be causing problems while failing to provide what is needed, so people try to compensate with supplements or additional foods.
That becomes a vicious circle: more food, more supplements, and yet health problems accumulate with age.
Then at a certain age people are routinely told to take preventive medications. Our approach takes a different direction.
We ask what is genuinely suitable for the human body and what the digestive system can process and make use of.
We also ask whether food can be handled without unnecessarily provoking the immune system.
The digestive tract is several meters long and contains many immune cells and lymphoid structures.
These include Peyer's patches and mesenteric lymph nodes, which I think of as guards monitoring what enters the body.
The respiratory system and lungs also have major immune defenses.
I believe diet can influence those systems, although the mechanisms are complex and should not be reduced to one simple cause.
Lung cancer, for example, has been strongly associated with smoking, but not every patient has smoked.
Other explanations such as passive smoke and pollution are then discussed.
My point is that many possible factors are considered, while diet is often not discussed in the way I think it should be.
The same applies to respiratory illnesses ranging from allergies to pneumonia and COVID-related illness.
I believe food deserves more attention. As a simple example, I often point to a child eating pizza late at night...
with cola and then coughing or developing other symptoms overnight.
I have associated symptoms such as feverishness, bed-wetting, or speech difficulties with what was eaten before sleep, although these observations require careful medical evaluation.
In my framework, I would say that pizza and cola can burden the body for days.
I designed the Al-Tayyibat System as what I consider a recovery-oriented system rather than merely a preventive diet, especially for people who already have health complaints.
I also do not treat obesity as the cause of all other illnesses; I regard obesity and other conditions as parallel outcomes rather than one necessarily causing the other.
A thin person can have many of the same complaints as an overweight person. In my view, the issue is not simply body weight but nutrition and absorption.
Both overweight and thin people can be poorly nourished. From my observations, I even felt some thin patients had more psychological complaints than heavier patients.
That was simply an observation, not a rule; different people respond differently.
I used to ask patients why their hair was falling out, and many would say it had been happening since they were young.
I would ask why menstruation had always been painful, and they would answer that this had been normal since puberty. I questioned the assumption that this must be normal.
A woman is not meant, in my view, to spend every month suffering from the time of puberty until old age.
A week of menstruation plus another week of premenstrual symptoms can consume half the month. That raised another question for me, as did fibroids.
Joint pain, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and other conditions also became questions that I tried to connect with lifestyle and diet.
I also discussed historical claims about when cancers were first documented and compared them with changes in food processing, though such historical claims need independent verification.
The Al-Tayyibat System developed, in my view, as both a recovery and preventive approach.
I came to present it as a comprehensive dietary system. We removed flour and soda and then extended the exclusions.
We excluded many raw and cooked vegetables, especially certain fibrous or legume-based foods and leafy vegetables.
We also excluded many seeds and husks. I questioned the use of psyllium husk simply to address bloating or bowel symptoms.
In my view, focusing only on shrinking or filling the stomach misses the question of what food is actually suitable for digestion.
So husks and seeds are generally excluded in our system.
Eggs, milk, and many dairy products are also excluded, including milk, creamers, and many fresh cheeses.
So what is eaten in Al-Tayyibat after removing all of those foods? One option we allow is certain whole-grain toast or whole-grain bread.
So what can you eat after removing all of those foods? In our system, one permitted option is certain whole-grain toast or whole-grain bread.
We allow many forms of whole grains, including wheat and rice. Wheat can be eaten as whole-grain dishes such as freekeh.
It can also be eaten as boiled whole wheat without milk. Rice can be white, brown, Thai, Egyptian, and prepared in various ways.
Corn can be eaten as popcorn, corn on the cob, or sweet corn. In our system, whole grains are treated as a major foundation.
Next in importance, after the bread or toast and grains, comes another major component that we do not ignore.
That component is fat. If I say life is supported by grains, I also consider fat an essential part of nourishment.
I do not accept the idea that fat should automatically be blamed for disease, fatty liver, or obesity.
I have used examples of undernourished people who are very thin yet have abdominal swelling and liver disease despite having little dietary fat.
They may be living on very limited foods or humanitarian food supplies such as refined flour, without rich sources of fat.
So I do not think visible obesity or liver problems automatically prove that dietary fat is the cause. In our system we use cream, butter, ghee...
and olive oil, with olive oil especially valued. I regard it as one of the best oils.
I have also argued that olive oil can solidify in the refrigerator and used that observation in discussing saturated and unsaturated fats.
From that, I concluded that common public messages about fats can sometimes be inconsistent.
So our permitted foods include certain whole-grain breads, rice, wheat, corn, fats, and then selected cheeses.
We include some processed or cooked cheeses, even those made with palm oil or hydrogenated fats; I do not treat the term 'hydrogenated' alone as automatically disqualifying.
I describe hydrogenation in chemical terms and argue that the body can handle many different fats, although this is one of the claims that should be independently evaluated.
Examples of cheeses we allow include varieties such as kashkaval, Emmental, Edam, Gouda, and aged Gouda.
Fruit is also included, but I rank fruits differently. Grapes, figs, bananas, dates, and plums are among the fruits I favor.
I consider these especially versatile because they can be eaten fresh and also used as fresh juices.
They can also be made into jam. We generally allow packaged juices as well, and I do not focus heavily on preservatives.
I have argued that common preservatives such as sodium nitrite, sodium benzoate, and monosodium glutamate are salts.
I have said that such compounds are usually handled and excreted by the body, so I do not place major emphasis on preservatives.
In our system, juices, jams, and many sweets are therefore allowed, based on that interpretation.
Many traditional sweets are allowed, with some exceptions. Likewise, I do not regard ordinary sugar as the main problem.
I am more concerned about artificial sweeteners than ordinary white sugar, which has been consumed historically for a very long time.
I describe refined sugar simply as concentrated cane juice and therefore do not consider sugar itself inherently harmful.
Even people with diabetes in our program may still consume some sugar. Meat is another category that I rank by texture and fiber length.
I also consider how much fat is present within the meat. In my ranking, lamb and young goat are among the easiest meats to deal with.
Next I place small birds such as pigeon, quail, and similar poultry.
After that comes fish, especially fish with soft flesh; I particularly favor sea fish.
I mention species such as grouper, sea bream, and similar fish. I am more cautious about farmed fish because of concerns about how they may be fed.
I have observed that some patients report sensitivities or other problems with certain farmed fish.
After that, liver is another meat I consider relatively soft and easy to digest.
Next in my ranking comes camel meat from certain softer cuts.
I consider camel meat nutritious and not especially difficult on digestion. After that comes veal or young buffalo meat.
These are relatively tender meats. The toughest, in my ranking, is meat from older cattle.
That is why I prefer softer cuts that can be boiled or braised until tender.
By contrast, in our system we generally exclude chicken, duck, turkey, goose, and similar large poultry.
We also exclude shrimp and squid. Crab and lobster are treated differently because, although they are shellfish, they contain larger pieces of soft meat.
I do not consider shrimp or squid to provide that same kind of meat. As an example of an Al-Tayyibat breakfast, we might have our permitted toast with...
processed cheese such as cheddar or Gouda, plus chips or fried potatoes with ketchup and mayonnaise.
Or mashed potatoes with butter. If you want something sweet afterward, the same toast can be eaten with cream...
and honey, or with halva or another permitted spread. That would already be more than enough for breakfast.
For lunch, something simple such as rice, soup, and a piece of meat, or rice with fish, is more than enough.
I do not think protein has to be eaten every day; even once a week can be enough in my framework.
What matters more to me is having the permitted bread or grains at breakfast and rice or grains at lunch. If you want a third, fourth, or fifth meal, that is up to you.
The only signal I want you to follow is your body's desire: if you are hungry, eat; if you are thirsty, drink.
Even if you drink water many times in a day, do not force yourself to eat simply because a scheduled mealtime has arrived, and do not force arbitrary water targets.
Your main guide should be genuine hunger and thirst. Over time, I believe the body adjusts to this pattern.
I also reflect on fasting: Ramadan fasting is thirty consecutive days rather than just a few scattered days in the month.
In my interpretation, the consecutive period initially challenges the body and then allows it to adapt by the end of the month.
After the first few days, the body adjusts to a different metabolic pattern, including increased production of ketone bodies.
Fat burning may increase relative to glucose use, and those metabolic changes continue developing through the later part of the fast.
I describe the month of fasting as a kind of periodic maintenance period for the body, including the liver.
For that reason, the Al-Tayyibat approach also includes periods of several hours without food or drink.
I believe such breaks can help the body regulate itself rather than constantly being fed.
We often push food on people—the woman who has just given birth, the child who looks tired, or the person who is sick—but I question that habit.
If a sick person has a fever and no appetite, I do not force food on them.
When a patient tells me, 'I am hungry,' I take that as a sign that they may be beginning to recover; similarly, thirst can signal improvement.
In my interpretation, the immune system has reduced its emergency response and allowed the digestive system to become active again.
The central idea is therefore to let the body's own signals and needs guide the process rather than mechanically following a diet plan simply because it was written down.
